<div class="abstract">
**Abstract.** EcoPhyloSim simulates the joint ecological and evolutionary dynamics
of a species community in space. Individuals on a grid die and are replaced by
offspring that disperse locally or globally, inherit and evolve traits, and are
selected by the environment and by competition with their neighbors, while new
species arise by speciation. The simulation records the spatial distribution of
the species, their traits and their phylogeny. This vignette gives an overview
of the model, describes each process with its equations and the patterns it
produces, and then shows the patterns of the community that emerge from the
processes together, compared with expectations from theory and earlier
studies. How to run the model and analyze its output is
shown in the vignette "EcoPhyloSim user guide"
(`vignette("PhyloSimManual", package = "EcoPhyloSim")`),
and how the patterns changed between releases in the vignette "Model history"
(`vignette("ModelHistory", package = "EcoPhyloSim")`).
</div>

# Overview

## Purpose and patterns

EcoPhyloSim is an individual-based, spatially explicit simulation of a species
community, meant to study how ecological processes (dispersal limitation,
environmental filtering and density dependence) and speciation together shape
the patterns of species communities: species richness and abundances, the
spatial distribution of the species, their traits and their phylogeny. The
processes can be switched on separately or combined, so their effects can be
compared with each other and with the neutral model, in which all individuals
are equivalent. The patterns are related to those that the plot and summary functions of
the package compute from the simulated community (see the vignette
"EcoPhyloSim user guide").

## Entities, state variables and scales

**The grid:** the simulation runs on a spatially discrete grid. Each cell is
occupied by one individual at any time. Each cell has an environmental value
(see Environmental filtering). To avoid boundary effects, the boundaries of the grid
are wrapped (torus).

**Individuals:** each individual has three traits in $[0, 1]$: an
environmental trait, a competition trait and a neutral trait. They change
from parent to offspring (see Trait evolution).

**Species and phylogeny:** each individual belongs to a species. The traits
of a species are the means of the traits of its individuals; they attract the
traits of the offspring (see Trait evolution). Each species also records its
parent species, which gives the phylogeny.

**Scales:** space is measured in cells and time in generations; in one
generation, as many individuals die as there are cells.

**Initial state:** at the start, all individuals belong to one species and all
their traits are 0.5.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x`, `y` | grid dimensions (cells) | 50, 50 | integers $\ge 1$, $x \cdot y \ge 2$ |
| `airmat` | environment of the cells (see Environmental filtering) | 1 (default gradient) | single value or matrix with $y$ rows and $x$ columns, values in $[0, 1]$ |

Table: Arguments of `createCompletePar()` for the grid and its environment.

## Process overview and scheduling

The simulation runs over a defined number of generations. In each generation,
cells are drawn at random until $x \cdot y$ individuals have died, and each
dead individual is replaced by the offspring of a parent (figure). The
processes act at these steps; the next chapter describes them in this order:

- **Dispersal:** the parent is drawn from the whole grid or from a
  neighborhood of the dead individual.
- **Trait evolution:** the offspring inherits the species and the traits of
  its parent, and its traits change slightly.
- **Environmental filtering** and **Density dependence:** each individual
  gets fitness terms.
- **Selection:** the fitness terms act on mortality (which individual dies),
  reproduction or recruitment (which parent replaces it).
- **Speciation:** at the end of each generation, new species arise.

The state of the community is recorded if the generation is one of those given
in `runs`.

```{r schema, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "One generation of the model. Deaths and replacements are repeated until x · y individuals have died; then new species arise, and the state is recorded at the generations given in runs."}
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-0.5, 10.3), ylim = c(0.3, 7), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
box3 <- function(x, y, label, w = 4.2, h = 0.75, col = "#e8f0f7") {
  rect(x - w / 2, y - h / 2, x + w / 2, y + h / 2, col = col, border = "#0072B2")
  text(x, y, label, cex = 0.75)
}
ys <- c(6.3, 5.1, 3.9, 2.7, 1.5)
box3(2.6, ys[1], "Draw a random cell")
box3(2.6, ys[2], "Does the individual die?\nprobability from its fitness")
box3(2.6, ys[3], "Choose a parent\nglobal or dispersal kernel (and fitness)")
box3(2.6, ys[4], "Offspring inherits species and traits;\ntraits evolve")
box3(2.6, ys[5], "Update the similarities\nof the neighbors")
box3(7.6, 3.9, "Speciation:\nPoisson(specRate) new species", col = "#fbeee6")
box3(7.6, 2.7, "Record the state\n(generations in runs)", col = "#fbeee6")
arrows(2.6, ys[-5] - 0.38, 2.6, ys[-1] + 0.38, length = 0.07)
# survives: draw the next cell
segments(0.5, ys[2], 0.2, ys[2]); segments(0.2, ys[2], 0.2, ys[1])
arrows(0.2, ys[1], 0.5, ys[1], length = 0.07)
text(0.2, mean(ys[1:2]), "survives", srt = 90, cex = 0.65, pos = 2, offset = 0.3)
# repeat until x * y individuals have died, then speciation
segments(4.7, ys[5], 5.1, ys[5]); segments(5.1, ys[5], 5.1, ys[1])
arrows(5.1, ys[1], 4.7, ys[1], length = 0.07)
text(5.15, 5.4, "repeat until\nx · y deaths", cex = 0.65, pos = 4)
arrows(5.1, 3.9, 5.5, 3.9, length = 0.07)
arrows(7.6, 3.52, 7.6, 3.08, length = 0.07)
# next generation
segments(7.6, 2.32, 7.6, 0.6); segments(7.6, 0.6, 9.85, 0.6); segments(9.85, 0.6, 9.85, 6.85)
segments(9.85, 6.85, 2.6, 6.85); arrows(2.6, 6.85, 2.6, 6.68, length = 0.07)

```{r patterns-setup, echo = FALSE}
data("packageBehavior")
main <- packageBehavior$main
gens <- packageBehavior$info$modes$main$generations # generations per block
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
# end of the figure captions: replicates, run length and the meaning of the symbols
reps <- packageBehavior$info$modes$main$reps
# fewer: tree statistics undefined in some runs (fewer than three species)
capRuns <- function(block, ref = TRUE, fewer = FALSE)
  paste0(sprintf("Lines or points: means of %d replicate runs at generation %s", reps, fmt(gens[[block]])),
         if (fewer) " (fewer for tree statistics in some settings; see Simulation design)",
         "; bands or bars: 95% confidence intervals",
         if (ref) "; open circle: reference setting" , ".")

labels <- c(richness = "Species richness", shannon = "Shannon diversity",
            conspecificNeighbors = "Conspecific neighbors",
            corTraitEnv = "Cor(trait, env.)",
            sdCompetitionTrait = "SD comp. trait",
            colless = "Colless index", gamma = "Gamma statistic",
            evenness = "Evenness", dominance = "Dominance", sdNeutralTrait = "SD neutral trait")
core <- names(labels)[1:7] # indicators shown by default
# colors: Okabe & Ito for unordered groups, a sequential palette for ordered
# values, global dispersal always grey
cols <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9")
groupCols <- function(v, levels = NULL) {
  v <- unique(as.character(v))
  num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(v))
  if (!all(!is.na(num) | v == "global")) return(setNames(rep(cols, length.out = length(v)), v))
  # ordered values: "global" first, then by value; with `levels` (e.g. all values
  # of dispersal), each value keeps its color in all figures
  v <- c(v[v == "global"], v[!is.na(num)][order(num[!is.na(num)])])
  lev <- if (is.null(levels)) v else levels
  pal <- setNames(hcl.colors(sum(lev != "global") + 1, "Viridis")[seq_len(sum(lev != "global"))],
                  lev[lev != "global"])
  setNames(c(global = "grey50", pal)[v], v)
}
dispersalLevels <- c("global", "0.5", "1", "2", "3")

# common style of all figures from here on (set for each chunk by the hook)
style <- function(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 1.6, 0.6), ...)
  par(..., mar = mar, mgp = c(2.1, 0.55, 0), tcl = -0.3, las = 1, bty = "l", cex = 0.75,
      font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.9) # mfrow (in ...) resets cex, so it comes first
knitr::knit_hooks$set(style = function(before, options, envir) if (before) style())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(style = TRUE, fig.retina = 2)

# x axis with plain numbers (no scientific notation) on a log scale
logAxis <- function(side = 1) {
  at <- axTicks(side)
  axis(side, at = at, labels = vapply(at, format, "", big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))
}

# legend in an empty panel of a multi-panel figure
legendPanel <- function(...) {
  op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  plot.new()
  legend("center", bty = "n", cex = 0.95, ...)
}

# 95% confidence intervals as error bars
ciBars <- function(x, m, ci, col) {
  # skip intervals too short to draw (they give "zero-length arrow" warnings)
  ok <- is.finite(ci) & ci > 1e-3 * diff(par("usr")[3:4])
  arrows(x[ok], m[ok] - ci[ok], x[ok], m[ok] + ci[ok], angle = 90, code = 3,
         length = 0.02, col = col)
}

# setting number of a block with the given parameter values
settingId <- function(d, block, ...) {
  s <- d$settings[d$settings$block == block, ]
  v <- list(...)
  for (n in names(v)) s <- s[s[[n]] == v[[n]], ]
  s$setting
}

# replicate mean and 95% confidence interval at the last census of each setting
final <- function(d, block, indicator) {
  x <- d$census[d$census$block == block & d$census$indicator == indicator, ]
  x <- x[x$generation == ave(x$generation, x$setting, FUN = max), ]
  x$ci <- qt(0.975, pmax(x$n - 1, 1)) * x$sd / sqrt(x$n)
  merge(d$settings[d$settings$block == block, ], x[c("setting", "mean", "sd", "ci", "n")])
}

# rows of a table of settings that have the parameter values of the reference
# setting (marked in the figures; generations may differ)
refPars <- setdiff(names(main$settings), c("block", "setting", "generations"))
refKey <- do.call(paste, lapply(main$settings[main$settings$block == "dispersal" &
                                                main$settings$dispersal == "1", refPars], as.character))
isRef <- function(f) do.call(paste, lapply(f[refPars], as.character)) == refKey

# current names of parameters that the data set keeps under their names of release 0.3.1
parName <- function(p) {
  if (is.null(p)) return(p)
  n <- c(density = "negativeDD", densityCut = "negativeDDCut")
  unname(ifelse(p %in% names(n), n[p], p))
}

# indicators against a parameter (x-axis), one color per value of `group`;
# numeric x: line and 95% confidence band, categories: points and 95% intervals;
# open circle: reference setting
response <- function(d, block, xvar, group = NULL, indicators = core,
                     xlab = parName(xvar), log = "", settings = NULL, discrete = FALSE, xnames = NULL) {
  op <- style(mfrow = c(2, ceiling((length(indicators) + 1) / 2)), mar = c(2, 3.4, 1.6, 1.2),
              oma = c(1.6, 0, 0, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  anyRef <- FALSE
  for (ind in indicators) {
    f <- final(d, block, ind)
    if (!is.null(settings)) f <- f[f$setting %in% settings, ]
    # order by the x value (non-numeric values such as "global" first), then by setting
    key <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(f[[xvar]]))
    key[is.na(key)] <- -Inf
    f <- f[order(key, f$setting), ]
    xv <- f[[xvar]]
    isFactor <- discrete || is.character(xv)
    if (isFactor) xv <- match(xv, unique(xv))
    g <- if (is.null(group)) rep("", nrow(f)) else as.character(f[[group]])
    gc <- if (is.null(group)) c("#0072B2") else
      groupCols(g, if (group == "dispersal") dispersalLevels)
    if (is.null(group)) names(gc) <- ""
    if (isFactor) xv <- xv + 0.08 * (match(g, names(gc)) - (length(gc) + 1) / 2) # side by side
    yr <- range(c(f$mean - f$ci, f$mean + f$ci), na.rm = TRUE)
    if (!all(is.finite(yr))) yr <- c(0, 1)
    plot(xv, f$mean, type = "n", ylim = yr, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = labels[ind],
         log = log, xaxt = "n")
    if (isFactor) {
      lab <- unique(f[[xvar]])
      axis(1, at = seq_along(lab), labels = FALSE)
      if (!is.null(xnames)) lab <- xnames[as.character(lab)]
      # long labels alternate between two lines, so that all are shown
      mtext(lab, side = 1, at = seq_along(lab), cex = par("cex"),
            line = if (sum(nchar(lab)) > 10) 0.4 + 0.8 * (seq_along(lab) %% 2 == 0) else 0.4)
    }
    else if (grepl("x", log)) logAxis(1) else axis(1)
    for (k in seq_along(gc)) {
      sel <- g == names(gc)[k]
      if (!isFactor && sum(sel) > 1) {
        ok <- sel & is.finite(f$ci)
        polygon(c(xv[ok], rev(xv[ok])), c(f$mean[ok] - f$ci[ok], rev(f$mean[ok] + f$ci[ok])),
                col = adjustcolor(gc[k], 0.2), border = NA)
        lines(xv[sel], f$mean[sel], col = gc[k], lwd = 1.5)
      } else ciBars(xv[sel], f$mean[sel], f$ci[sel], gc[k])
      points(xv[sel], f$mean[sel], col = gc[k], pch = 16)
    }
    r <- isRef(f)
    points(xv[r], f$mean[r], pch = 1, cex = 1.8)
    anyRef <- anyRef || any(r)
  }
  mtext(xlab, side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.4, cex = 0.75)
  ng <- if (is.null(group)) 0 else length(gc)
  if (ng || anyRef)
    legendPanel(legend = c(names(gc)[seq_len(ng)], if (anyRef) "reference setting"),
                col = c(gc[seq_len(ng)], if (anyRef) "black"), pch = c(rep(16, ng), if (anyRef) 1),
                lty = c(rep(if (isFactor) 0 else 1, ng), if (anyRef) 0), lwd = 1.5,
                pt.cex = c(rep(1, ng), if (anyRef) 1.8), title = parName(group))
}

# replicate mean (line) and mean +/- sd (band) of each indicator over time
trajectories <- function(d, cases, indicators = core) {
  op <- style(mfrow = c(2, ceiling((length(indicators) + 1) / 2)), mar = c(2, 3.4, 1.6, 1.2),
              oma = c(1.6, 0, 0, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (ind in indicators) {
    x <- d$census[d$census$indicator == ind, ]
    sub <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(cases)), function(k)
      x[x$block == cases$block[k] & x$setting == cases$setting[k], ])
    yr <- range(unlist(lapply(sub, function(s) c(s$mean - s$sd, s$mean + s$sd))), na.rm = TRUE)
    plot(1, type = "n", log = "x", xlim = range(x$generation), ylim = yr,
         xlab = "", ylab = "", main = labels[ind], xaxt = "n")
    logAxis(1)
    for (k in seq_along(sub)) {
      s <- sub[[k]][order(sub[[k]]$generation), ]
      ok <- is.finite(s$sd)
      polygon(c(s$generation[ok], rev(s$generation[ok])),
              c(s$mean[ok] - s$sd[ok], rev(s$mean[ok] + s$sd[ok])),
              col = adjustcolor(cases$col[k], 0.2), border = NA)
      lines(s$generation, s$mean, col = cases$col[k], lwd = 1.5)
    }
  }
  mtext("Generation", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.4, cex = 0.75)
  legendPanel(legend = cases$label, col = cases$col, lwd = 2)
}

# adds the settings of another block (e.g. the reference setting) to a block, for
# a figure; the added settings get new setting numbers in that block
withSettings <- function(d, block, from, ...) {
  s <- d$settings[d$settings$block == from, ]
  v <- list(...)
  for (n in names(v)) s <- s[s[[n]] %in% v[[n]], ]
  x <- d$census[d$census$block == from & d$census$setting %in% s$setting, ]
  new <- max(d$settings$setting[d$settings$block == block]) + seq_len(nrow(s))
  x$setting <- new[match(x$setting, s$setting)]
  s$setting <- new
  s$block <- x$block <- block
  d$settings <- rbind(d$settings, s)
  d$census <- rbind(d$census, x)
  d
}

# neutral theory for J individuals and specRate new species per generation:
# speciation probability per replacement nu = specRate / J and
# theta = (J - 1) nu / (1 - nu) (Vallade & Houchmandzadeh 2003, eq. 6)
theta <- function(specRate, J) (J - 1) * (specRate / J) / (1 - specRate / J)
# expected species richness (Ewens sampling formula)
ewens <- function(theta, J) sum(theta / (theta + 0:(J - 1)))
# expected rank-abundance curve: mean of sorted abundances of random
# Ewens partitions (Hoppe urn); like the simulated curves, each rank is
# averaged over the partitions that have at least that many species
ewensRac <- function(theta, J, reps = 200) {
  racs <- replicate(reps, {
    sp <- integer(J)
    n <- 0
    for (i in seq_len(J)) {
      if (runif(1) < theta / (theta + i - 1)) {
        n <- n + 1
        sp[i] <- n
      } else sp[i] <- sp[sample.int(i - 1, 1)]
    }
    sort(tabulate(sp), decreasing = TRUE)
  }, simplify = FALSE)
  len <- max(lengths(racs))
  rowMeans(sapply(racs, function(r) c(r, rep(NA, len - length(r)))), na.rm = TRUE)
}
# replicate mean of an indicator at the last census, for the setting of a block
# with the given parameter values (for the text)
val <- function(block, indicator, ..., digits = 2) {
  f <- final(main, block, indicator)
  signif(f$mean[f$setting == settingId(main, block, ...)], digits)
}
```

## Time to equilibrium

A simulation starts with a single species whose individuals all have the same
traits, so the indicators change until the model reaches equilibrium. The time
this takes, and in the next section the runtime, are shown with the runs of the
simulation design (see Simulation design below; `r reps` replicate runs per
setting), here for five settings.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the neutral model, abundances change only by drift, which
is slower in larger communities. We therefore expect the time to equilibrium
to grow with the number of cells, and to be longer for indicators that depend
on the whole history of the community (the phylogeny) than for those that
depend on the current abundances.
:::

```{r equilibrium, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste0("Indicators over time (logarithmic axis) for five settings: neutral model with global dispersal on 50 × 50 cells (specRate = 2) and on 100 × 100 cells (specRate = 0.5), and with dispersal 1 without other processes, with environment = 1 and with negativeDD = 1 (50 × 50 cells, specRate = 2). Line: mean of ", reps, " replicate runs; band: mean ± standard deviation across replicates. The neutral runs last ", fmt(gens[["neutral"]]), " generations, the run with density dependence ", fmt(gens[["density"]]), " and the others ", fmt(gens[["dispersal"]]), ".")}
cases <- data.frame(
  block = c("neutral", "neutral", "dispersal", "environment", "density"),
  setting = c(settingId(main, "neutral", specRate = 2, x = 50),
              settingId(main, "neutral", specRate = 0.5, x = 100),
              settingId(main, "dispersal", dispersal = "1"),
              settingId(main, "environment", environment = 1, dispersal = "1"),
              settingId(main, "density", density = 1, densityCut = 1)),
  label = c("neutral, global", "neutral, global,\n100 × 100,\nspecRate 0.5",
            "neutral, dispersal 1", "environment 1", "negativeDD 1"),
  col = c("grey50", "grey20", cols[1:3]))
trajectories(main, cases)
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Species richness, Shannon diversity and the share of
conspecific neighbors level off within a few thousand generations (in the
neutral model on 50 × 50 cells after about 2,000–4,000 generations). The gamma statistic, and in some settings the Colless index
and the spread of the competition trait, take longer, up to tens of thousands
of generations. On 100 × 100 cells with
`specRate = 0.5`, the tree statistics settle only after more than 80,000
generations, as expected for a larger community with fewer new species. The
correlation between trait and environment has no meaning without
environmental filtering.
:::

## Runtime

The runtime depends on the number of cells, the dispersal distance and the
neighborhood of density dependence. It was recorded for all runs of the
design.

```{r runtime-setup, echo = FALSE}
# replicate mean runtime of the core simulation per setting
rt <- merge(main$settings, main$runtime)
rt$per1000 <- rt$mean / rt$generations * 1000
# runtime per 1,000 generations of the setting of a block with the given parameter values
rtVal <- function(block, ..., digits = 2) {
  d <- rt[rt$block == block, ]
  v <- list(...)
  for (n in names(v)) d <- d[d[[n]] == v[[n]], ]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(NA)
  signif(d$per1000, digits)
}
```

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In each generation, as many individuals die and are replaced as there are
cells, so the runtime grows with the number of cells. Each replacement looks at the
cells within the dispersal kernel and, with density dependence, at the
neighborhood of the recruit, so larger kernels and neighborhoods take longer.
:::

```{r runtime-text, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
fold <- function(cut) {
  d <- rt[rt$block == "density" & rt$densityCut == cut, ]
  round(max(d$per1000) / d$per1000[d$density == 0], 1)
}
cat(sprintf(
"The figure shows the runtime of the core simulation per 1,000 generations in
the runs of the simulation design (replicate means; each simulation on one core of a
desktop PC, several in parallel). Runtimes on other computers differ, but the ratios
between settings should be similar. On 50 × 50 cells,
global dispersal is fastest (%s seconds per 1,000 generations). With local
dispersal, the runtime increases steeply with the dispersal distance (from %s
seconds at 0.5 to %s seconds at 3). With dispersal 1, it grows somewhat faster
than the number of cells. Density dependence increases it by a factor of up to
about %s with neighborhood radius 1 and %s with radius 2, almost independently
of its strength. Together with the time to
equilibrium, this gives the cost of a simulation: e.g. 50,000 generations on
100 × 100 cells with dispersal 1 take about %s minutes.
",
rtVal("dispersal", dispersal = "global"), rtVal("dispersal", dispersal = "0.5"),
rtVal("dispersal", dispersal = "3"), fold(1), fold(2), round(rtVal("gridSize", x = 100) * 50 / 60)))
```

```{r runtime, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6, fig.cap = "Runtime of the core simulation in seconds per 1,000 generations against the dispersal kernel (50 × 50 cells), the number of cells (dispersal 1) and the strength of density dependence (dispersal 1, two neighborhood radii)."}
op <- style(mfrow = c(1, 3))
d <- rt[rt$block == "dispersal", ]
d <- d[match(c("global", "0.5", "1", "2", "3"), d$dispersal), ]
plot(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$per1000, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[1], xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Dispersal", ylab = "Seconds per 1,000 generations")
axis(1, at = seq_len(nrow(d)), labels = d$dispersal)
d <- rt[rt$block == "gridSize", ]
d <- d[order(d$x), ]
plot(d$x^2, d$per1000, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[1], log = "xy", xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Cells", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = d$x^2, labels = format(d$x^2, big.mark = ","))
d <- rt[rt$block == "density", ]
plot(range(d$density), range(d$per1000), type = "n", xlab = "negativeDD",
     ylab = "")
dc <- groupCols(1:2)
for (k in 1:2) {
  dk <- d[d$densityCut == k, ]
  dk <- dk[order(dk$density), ]
  lines(dk$density, dk$per1000, type = "b", pch = 16, col = dc[k])
}
legend("bottomright", legend = paste("negativeDDCut", 1:2), col = dc, lty = 1, pch = 16, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

## Simulation design

The patterns in the next two chapters show how the main outputs of the
model respond to its parameters, compared with what theory and earlier studies
lead us to expect. For the neutral model, some expectations are exact analytical
results; for the other processes, the literature mostly predicts the direction
of an effect. The parameters are varied one or two at a time around a reference
setting (50 × 50 cells, `dispersal = 1`, `specRate = 2`, all other parameters
at their defaults), with `r packageBehavior$info$modes$main$reps` replicate
runs per setting. The simulations take days, so they are not run when this
vignette is built: they were run with the scripts in
`PhyloSim/data-raw/model-behavior` of the
[package repository](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim) at
the commit `r packageBehavior$info$commit`, and their summaries are stored in
the data set `packageBehavior` (see `?packageBehavior`). The same design is run
with every release; how the patterns changed between releases is shown in the
vignette "Model history".
The data set keeps the names of release 0.3.1 (`density`, `densityCut`); text
and figures use the current names.

The indicators are computed for the whole grid at each census: species
richness, Shannon diversity, the share of the four neighbors of a cell that
belong to the same species (spatial aggregation), the correlation between the
environmental trait and the environment, the standard deviation of the
competition trait, and the Yule-normalized Colless index and the gamma
statistic of the tree of the extant species. Further indicators (evenness,
dominance, the spread of the neutral trait, the height of the tree, species
ages and the phylogenetic dispersion of local plots) are in the data set and
are used where they help. Each pattern is first stated as an expectation (blue
boxes) and then compared with the simulations (green boxes).

**Reading the figures.** Most figures show one indicator per panel at the end
of the runs against the parameter named below the panels; the captions say what
lines, bands and symbols show. Colors separate a second parameter: ordered
values from dark to light, unordered groups in distinct colors, global
dispersal in grey. The tree statistics (Colless index, gamma) and
the correlation between species age and abundance need at least three species;
where runs ended with fewer, their means are over fewer replicates (down to 2
of `r reps` for protracted speciation over 5 generations).

Each setting was simulated for `r fmt(gens[["dispersal"]])` generations, the
settings of the section Density dependence for `r fmt(gens[["density"]])` and the
neutral model for `r fmt(gens[["neutral"]])` generations, with censuses spaced
logarithmically over the run and densely in its second half.

# Processes

Each section describes a process with its equations and parameters, and then
shows the patterns specific to it. The symbols refer to the arguments of
`createCompletePar()`; the tables give their default values and the ranges that
`createCompletePar()` and `runSimulation()` check (see also
`?createCompletePar`).

## Dispersal

The dead individual is replaced by the offspring of a parent. With global
dispersal, the parent is drawn uniformly from all other cells. With local dispersal, it is drawn from the
cells within the radius $R$ (excluding the cell itself), with weights

$$ K(d) = \exp\left(-\frac{d}{\delta}\right), $$

where $d$ is the Euclidean distance, $R = \lfloor 2 \cdot \texttt{dispersal}
\rfloor$ and $\delta = R / 2$. For multiples of 0.5, $\delta$ = `dispersal`, the
distance at which the weight falls to $1/e$; other values act like the next
lower multiple of 0.5 (see Known limitations). The neighborhood is a discretized circle: all cells with
$|\Delta x| \le R$ and $|\Delta y| \le \lfloor\sqrt{R^2 - \Delta x^2}\rfloor$.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dispersal` | `"global"` (or 0), or the dispersal distance | `"global"` | `"global"`, 0 or $\ge 0.5$ with $2R + 1 \le \min(x, y)$ |

Table: Argument of `createCompletePar()` for dispersal.

`dispersal` sets how far offspring settle from their parent. The simulations
vary it from 0.5 to 3 cells and compare it with global dispersal.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With local dispersal, offspring settle near their parents, so
conspecifics form spatial clusters [@chaveleigh2002] and the share of
conspecific neighbors increases. Lineages in different parts of the grid stay
apart longer before they replace each other, so we expect more species on the
whole grid than with global dispersal. With local dispersal, small subplots
should contain fewer species than random samples of the same size, because
conspecifics are clustered, and the species–area curve within the grid should be flatter at small areas
and steeper at large areas, where further clusters are added; with global
dispersal, subplots are random samples of the whole grid, so the curve rises
fast at small areas and flattens as it approaches the richness of the grid
[@chave2002]. In spatial neutral models, species–area curves for different
dispersal distances coincide once area is rescaled by the dispersal distance
[@rosindell2007]. The probability that two individuals at a given distance belong
to the same species should decrease with distance when dispersal is limited
[@chaveleigh2002; @condit2002]; with global dispersal, it should be the same at
all distances and equal to the neutral expectation $1/(1+\theta)$.
:::

```{r dispersal, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators at the end of the runs against the dispersal distance (global: the parent is drawn from the whole grid), on 50 × 50 cells with specRate = 2, without environmental filtering or density dependence.", capRuns("dispersal"))}
response(main, "dispersal", "dispersal")
```

```{r dispersal-sac, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Species–area curves within the grid for different dispersal distances, at the end of the runs of the previous figure: mean number of species in randomly placed square subplots against their area (both axes logarithmic; replicate means)."}
s <- main$sac[main$sac$block == "dispersal", ]
st <- main$settings[main$settings$block == "dispersal", ]
dc <- groupCols(st$dispersal, dispersalLevels)
plot(s$size, s$mean, type = "n", log = "xy", xlab = "Subplot area (cells)",
     ylab = "Species")
for (k in seq_len(nrow(st))) {
  x <- s[s$setting == st$setting[k], ]
  x <- x[order(x$size), ]
  lines(x$size, x$mean, col = dc[k], type = "b", pch = 16)
}
legend("topleft", legend = st$dispersal, col = dc, lty = 1,
       pch = 16, title = "dispersal", bty = "n")
```

```{r dispersal-decay, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Probability that two cells at the given distance (along rows and columns) contain the same species, for different dispersal distances, at the end of the same runs (replicate mean and 95% confidence interval). Dashed: neutral expectation 1/(1 + θ) for global dispersal."}
s <- main$decay[main$decay$block == "dispersal", ]
s$ci <- qt(0.975, pmax(s$n - 1, 1)) * s$sd / sqrt(s$n)
plot(s$distance, s$mean, type = "n", log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Distance (cells)", ylab = "Same species")
for (k in seq_len(nrow(st))) {
  x <- s[s$setting == st$setting[k], ]
  x <- x[order(x$distance), ]
  polygon(c(x$distance, rev(x$distance)), c(x$mean - x$ci, rev(x$mean + x$ci)),
          col = adjustcolor(dc[k], 0.2), border = NA)
  lines(x$distance, x$mean, col = dc[k], type = "b", pch = 16)
}
abline(h = 1 / (1 + theta(2, 2500)), lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = st$dispersal, col = dc, lty = 1,
       pch = 16, title = "dispersal", bty = "n")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** As expected, shorter dispersal increases richness on the whole grid
(`r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "0.5", digits = 3)` species with
`dispersal = 0.5`, `r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "global", digits = 3)`
with global dispersal) and the share of conspecific neighbors. With local
dispersal, small subplots contain fewer species, so that, as expected, the
species–area curve is flatter at small areas and steeper at large areas than
with global dispersal. With local dispersal,
the probability that two cells contain the same species decreases with distance,
as expected.
With dispersal distances of 2 and 3 cells, richness is close to that with global
dispersal.
:::

## Trait evolution

The offspring inherits the species and the three traits
(environmental, competition and neutral trait) of its parent. Each trait then
changes by a small random step and is attracted towards the mean trait of its
species:

$$ t' = (1 - \alpha)\cdot t_{\mathrm{p}} + \alpha \cdot \bar t + r, $$

where $t'$ is the offspring's trait value, $t_{\mathrm{p}}$ the parent's,
$\bar t$ is the mean trait value of the species, $\alpha = 0.2$ is a fixed
attraction weight, and $r$ is drawn uniformly from $[-0.01, 0.01]$. Values outside $[0, 1]$ are reflected at the boundary.

## Environmental filtering

Environmental filtering and density dependence give each individual fitness
terms between 0 and 1, which act on mortality, reproduction or recruitment
(see Selection). Environmental filtering, with $e$ = `environment`:

$$ w_{E,i} = e \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(E_i - t_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) + 1 - e, $$

where $E_i$ is the environment of the cell, $t_i$ is the environmental trait
of the individual and $\sigma$ = `nicheWidth` is the width of the niche.

**Environment.** If no `airmat` is given, the environment varies only along the
x-axis: it is $1 - |2i/x - 1|$ in column $i = 0, \dots, x - 1$, i.e., it
increases linearly in steps of $2/x$ from 0 in the first column to its maximum in
the middle and then decreases again. The maximum is 1 for even $x$ and $(x-1)/x$
for odd $x$; for even $x$ all values except the minimum and maximum occur in two
bands. A user-defined environment can be
passed as a matrix with values in $[0, 1]$ (`airmat`).

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `environment` | weight $e$ of the environmental fitness term | 0 | $[0, 1]$ |
| `nicheWidth` | width $\sigma$ (standard deviation) of the environmental niche | 0.0366 (the value fixed in earlier versions) | $> 0$; a message outside $[0.003, 3]$ (if `environment` > 0) |

Table: Arguments of `createCompletePar()` for environmental filtering.

`environment` sets the weight of the environmental fitness term. The
simulations vary it from 0 to 1, with global dispersal and with dispersal 1.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Environmental filtering sorts species along the gradient, so
the correlation between trait and environment should increase with
`environment`. With local dispersal, offspring stay in the habitat of their
parents (species sorting); with global dispersal, many offspring land in
unsuitable cells (mass effects), which weakens the match between traits and
environment and reduces the differences between parts of the grid
[@mouquet2003]. The effect on richness can go either way: environmental
heterogeneity increases richness through niche partitioning in most empirical
studies [@stein2014], but in an area of fixed size, narrow niches reduce the
area available to each species and can reduce richness [@allouche2012]. For
tree shape, we found no consistent prediction.
:::

```{r environment, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the strength of environmental filtering (environment), with global dispersal and dispersal 1, on 50 × 50 cells with specRate = 2 and the default niche width.", capRuns("environment"))}
response(main, "environment", "environment", group = "dispersal")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** With local dispersal, already weak filtering (`environment = 0.25`)
makes the correlation between trait and environment almost perfect
(`r val("environment", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "1", environment = 0.25)`),
whereas with global dispersal it stays at
`r val("environment", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "global", environment = 1)` even
at `environment = 1`, as expected from mass effects. Richness increases with the
strength of filtering in both cases, so niche partitioning dominates over the
loss of area per species. Filtering makes the trees more balanced (Colless index
below 0) and increases the gamma statistic, i.e. branching is even more
concentrated towards the present than in the neutral model. A possible
explanation is that lineages adapted to different parts of the gradient persist
for a long time, while species within each part turn over as in the neutral
model; the speciation rate does not depend on richness, so no slowdown of
branching is expected [@phillimore2008]. With global dispersal, filtering lowers
the share of conspecific neighbors; with local dispersal, it changes it little.
:::

### Niche width

The niche width `nicheWidth` sets how fast fitness declines when the
environmental trait of an individual differs from the environment of its cell.
The simulations vary it from 0.01 to 0.3 with full environmental filtering
(`environment = 1`), with global dispersal and with dispersal 1.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Narrower niches mean stronger filtering. Following the idea of
limiting similarity, more species with narrow niches can be packed along the
gradient, but narrow niches also reduce the area available to each species,
which increases the risk of extinction [@allouche2012]. Richness may therefore
peak at an intermediate niche width. The correlation between trait and
environment should be highest for narrow niches.
:::

```{r nichewidth, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the niche width (nicheWidth, logarithmic axis) with full environmental filtering (environment = 1), for global dispersal and dispersal 1 (50 × 50 cells, specRate = 2).", capRuns("nicheWidth", ref = FALSE))}
response(main, "nicheWidth", "nicheWidth", group = "dispersal", log = "x")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** With global dispersal, richness is highest at intermediate niche
widths, as expected, but the correlation between trait and environment increases
with niche width (from
`r val("nicheWidth", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "global", nicheWidth = 0.01)` to
`r val("nicheWidth", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "global", nicheWidth = 0.3)`).
A possible reason is that with narrow niches and global dispersal, almost all
offspring land in unsuitable cells, so that fitness is low everywhere and
filtering is weak. With
local dispersal, traits match the environment closely at all widths, and richness
is highest for the narrowest niches.
:::

## Density dependence

Density dependence makes fitness depend on how similar an individual is to its
neighbors: negative density dependence penalizes individuals that are similar
to their neighbors, positive density dependence those that are dissimilar.
With $c$ = `negativeDD` and $p$ = `positiveDD`, the fitness terms are

$$ w_{N,i} = 1 - c \cdot S_i, \qquad w_{P,i} = 1 - p \cdot (1 - S^{P}_i), $$

where $S_i$ and $S^{P}_i$ are the similarities of the individual to its
neighbors within the radius `negativeDDCut` or `positiveDDCut`. The
neighborhood is the discretized circle of the dispersal kernel without the
focal cell (4, 12 and 28 neighbors for radius 1, 2 and 3). The similarity is
the mean over the $n$ neighbors $j$ of

- `"absolute"` (default for negative density dependence): $1 - |a_i - a_j|$,
  where $a$ is the competition trait;
- `"gaussian"`: $\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a_i - a_j}{\omega}\right)^2\right)$,
  with $\omega$ = `negativeDDWidth` or `positiveDDWidth`;
- `"species"` (default for positive density dependence): 1 if $j$ belongs to
  the same species, 0 otherwise, i.e. the share of conspecific neighbors.

The similarities are updated whenever an individual in the neighborhood is
replaced.

Some consequences of these definitions:

- All individuals start as one species with the same traits (0.5), so density
  dependence acts only after the competition traits have diverged or new
  species have arisen (see Known limitations).
- Strengths are not directly comparable between kernels, as the distributions
  of the similarity differ.
- Positive density dependence is destabilizing and quickly leads to the
  dominance of a few species; it is meant to be combined with negative density
  dependence at another radius or with another kernel. With the same kernel,
  radius (and width of a Gaussian kernel), the two partly offset each other,
  which gives a message.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `negativeDD` | strength $c$ of negative density dependence (formerly `density`) | 0 | $[0, 1]$ |
| `negativeDDCut` | radius of its neighborhood (formerly `densityCut`) | 1 | integer $\ge 1$, $\le \min(x, y)$; $2 \cdot$ `negativeDDCut` $+ 1 \le \min(x, y)$ if `negativeDD` > 0 |
| `negativeDDKernel` | similarity measure | `"absolute"` | `"absolute"`, `"gaussian"`, `"species"` |
| `negativeDDWidth` | width $\omega$ of the Gaussian kernel | 0.1 | $> 0$; a message above 1 or below 0.001 |
| `negativeDDResponse` | experimental: the fitness term as a function of $S_i$ instead of $1 - c \cdot S_i$ | `"linear"` | `"linear"`, a function, or at least 2 values in $[0, 1]$ |
| `positiveDD` | experimental: strength $p$ of positive density dependence | 0 | $[0, 1]$ |
| `positiveDDCut`, `positiveDDKernel`, `positiveDDWidth` | as for negative density dependence | 1, `"species"`, 0.1 | as for negative density dependence |

Table: Arguments of `createCompletePar()` for density dependence.

### Negative density dependence

Negative density dependence is set by its strength `negativeDD` and the radius
`negativeDDCut` of the neighborhood. The simulations vary the strength from 0
to 1 for the radii 1 and 2.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With the default kernel (`"absolute"`), an individual is
fitter the more its competition trait differs from those of its neighbors.
Because the traits within a species are similar, this acts like conspecific
negative density dependence, but only
after the competition traits have diverged (see Known limitations). Such
density dependence is
expected to increase species richness and to make abundances more even
[@chave2002; @levi2019]. It should reduce the share of conspecific neighbors. Competition
on a trait favors dissimilar trait values, so the spread of the competition
trait should increase; species may form groups of similar trait values rather
than spreading evenly along the trait axis [@scheffer2006].
:::

```{r density, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the strength of negative density dependence (negativeDD, kernel \"absolute\") for the neighborhood radii 1 and 2 (negativeDDCut), with dispersal 1 on 50 × 50 cells (specRate = 2).", capRuns("density"))}
response(main, "density", "density", group = "densityCut")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Density dependence clearly reduces the share of conspecific
neighbors (with radius 1 from
`r val("density", "conspecificNeighbors", density = 0, densityCut = 1)` to
`r val("density", "conspecificNeighbors", density = 1, densityCut = 1)`, less with
radius 2), but it increases richness only slightly (from
`r val("density", "richness", density = 0, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)` to
`r val("density", "richness", density = 1, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)` species with
radius 1) and, contrary to the expectation, does not make abundances more even.
As expected, competition drives the traits apart, and they form groups: already
at `negativeDD = 0.25`, the standard deviation of the competition trait rises
from `r val("density", "sdCompetitionTrait", density = 0, densityCut = 1)` to
about `r val("density", "sdCompetitionTrait", density = 0.25, densityCut = 1)`,
close to its maximum of 0.5 on $[0, 1]$, i.e. the traits split into two groups
near 0 and 1. Species within each group have similar traits, so the trait kernel
hardly separates them, which is a likely reason for the small effect on
richness (see Similarity measure of density dependence). Density dependence
also increases the gamma statistic. Above 0.25, the strength changes the
patterns little, except that the share of conspecific neighbors keeps
decreasing.
:::

### Similarity measure of density dependence

The kernel `negativeDDKernel` sets how the similarity to the neighbors is
measured: by the competition trait (`"absolute"`, `"gaussian"`) or by species
identity (`"species"`). The simulations compare the three kernels at strengths
0.5 and 1 against no density dependence.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With `"species"`, the fitness term depends on the share
of conspecific neighbors, which corresponds to conspecific negative density
dependence as measured in field studies [@comita2010]; it acts from the first speciation on,
so we expect larger effects on richness and on the share of conspecific
neighbors than with the trait kernels (strengths are not directly
comparable between kernels, see above), and no selection on the
competition trait, whose spread should then be like that of the neutral trait.
The `"gaussian"` kernel with the default width 0.1 counts only neighbors with
similar traits, so it should act more like `"species"` once the traits of
species have diverged.
:::

```{r densitykernel, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the strength of negative density dependence for the three similarity measures (negativeDDKernel; radius 1, dispersal 1, 50 × 50 cells); the settings with the kernel \"absolute\" and without density dependence are those of the previous figure. The last panel shows the spread of the neutral trait instead of the correlation between trait and environment.", capRuns("densityKernel"))}
response(withSettings(main, "densityKernel", "density", density = c(0, 0.5, 1), densityCut = 1),
         "densityKernel", "density", group = "negativeDDKernel",
         indicators = c(core[-4], "sdNeutralTrait"))
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** The `"species"` kernel has by far the strongest effect: richness
rises from `r val("density", "richness", density = 0, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)`
species without density dependence to
`r val("densityKernel", "richness", negativeDDKernel = "species", density = 1, digits = 3)`
at strength 1 (`"absolute"`:
`r val("density", "richness", density = 1, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)`), the
share of conspecific neighbors falls to
`r val("densityKernel", "conspecificNeighbors", negativeDDKernel = "species", density = 1)`,
and abundances become much more even. As expected, the competition trait is not
under selection with this kernel: its spread is the same as that of the neutral
trait. The `"gaussian"` kernel lies in between
(`r val("densityKernel", "richness", negativeDDKernel = "gaussian", density = 1, digits = 3)`
species at strength 1). The spread of the competition trait is smaller than
with `"absolute"` (standard deviation
`r val("densityKernel", "sdCompetitionTrait", negativeDDKernel = "gaussian", density = 1)`),
but the kernel acts less like `"species"`
than expected, possibly because the traits of many species still differ by less
than the kernel width 0.1.
:::

### Density dependence and dispersal

Dispersal sets how far offspring settle relative to the neighborhood of density
dependence. The simulations vary `dispersal` from 0.5 to 3 cells and include
global dispersal, with full negative density dependence (`negativeDD = 1`,
radius 1, kernel `"absolute"`).

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** The effect of density dependence on diversity depends on how
far offspring disperse relative to the neighborhood of competition
[@adler2005]: with short dispersal, offspring settle among their relatives, so
density dependence acts mostly against the offspring of locally common species;
with global dispersal, they land among random neighbors.
:::

```{r densitydispersal, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against dispersal with full negative density dependence (negativeDD = 1, radius 1, kernel \"absolute\"; 50 × 50 cells, specRate = 2); the setting with dispersal 1 is that of Negative density dependence.", capRuns("densityDispersal", ref = FALSE))}
response(withSettings(main, "densityDispersal", "density", density = 1, densityCut = 1),
         "densityDispersal", "dispersal")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Density dependence increases richness most when
offspring settle close to their parents: with `dispersal = 0.5`, it gives
`r val("densityDispersal", "richness", dispersal = "0.5", digits = 3)` species
(`r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "0.5", digits = 3)` without density
dependence, see Dispersal), whereas with global dispersal, richness is about the
same with and without it
(`r val("densityDispersal", "richness", dispersal = "global", digits = 3)` and
`r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "global", digits = 3)`). It reduces the
share of conspecific neighbors at all dispersal distances. (Runs without density
dependence: 50,000 instead of 100,000 generations; see Time to equilibrium.)
:::

### Positive density dependence

`positiveDD` sets the strength of positive density dependence. The simulations use the `"species"` kernel with
radius 2 and strengths 0.01 and 0.05, alone and together with negative density
dependence (`negativeDD = 1`, kernel `"species"`, radius 1).

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Positive density dependence favors individuals surrounded by
conspecifics. We therefore expect fewer species, lower evenness and stronger spatial aggregation (see above). Combined with conspecific negative density dependence in
the 4 adjacent cells (radius 1) and positive density dependence within radius
2, conspecifics in the adjacent cells count against an individual and those
further out count for it. This may keep clusters at an intermediate size; we
found no prediction in the literature for this.
:::

```{r positivedd, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the strength of positive density dependence (kernel \"species\", radius 2), without and with negative density dependence (negativeDD = 1, kernel \"species\", radius 1); dispersal 1, 50 × 50 cells. The settings without positive density dependence are those of the sections Negative density dependence and Similarity measure of density dependence.", capRuns("positiveDD", fewer = TRUE))}
pd <- withSettings(main, "positiveDD", "density", density = 0, densityCut = 1)
pd <- withSettings(pd, "positiveDD", "densityKernel", density = 1, negativeDDKernel = "species")
response(pd, "positiveDD", "positiveDD", group = "density",
         indicators = c("richness", "evenness", "dominance", "conspecificNeighbors", "sdCompetitionTrait", "colless", "gamma"))
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Alone, positive density dependence leads to the dominance of a
single species, as expected: with `positiveDD = 0.01`, the most abundant
species holds on average
`r round(100 * val("positiveDD", "dominance", positiveDD = 0.01, density = 0))`% of
the individuals, richness falls from
`r val("density", "richness", density = 0, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)` to
`r val("positiveDD", "richness", positiveDD = 0.01, density = 0)` species
(`r val("positiveDD", "richness", positiveDD = 0.05, density = 0)` at 0.05), and
almost all neighbors are conspecific. Combined with negative density dependence,
positive density dependence at these strengths reduces richness only slightly
(`r val("positiveDD", "richness", positiveDD = 0.05, density = 1, digits = 3)`
species at 0.05 instead of
`r val("densityKernel", "richness", negativeDDKernel = "species", density = 1, digits = 3)`),
and the share of conspecific neighbors stays low: negative density dependence
dominates at these strengths. Whether clusters of intermediate size form cannot
be judged from the share of conspecific neighbors.
:::

## Selection

Cells are drawn at random (with replacement)
until $J = x \cdot y$ individuals have died, so some individuals die several
times per generation and others not at all. If fitness does not act on
mortality, every draw kills. If it does (`fitnessActsOn` is `"mortality"` or
`"both"`, or a combination with `"mortality"`, and `environment`, `negativeDD`, `positiveDD`, `redQueen` or
`redQueenStrength` is > 0), a drawn individual $i$ dies with probability $r_i / r_{\max}$, where
$r_{\max}$ is the largest possible value of the relative death rate

$$ r_i = \prod_j \left(1 + (m - 1)(1 - w_{ij})\right), $$

where the product runs over the mechanisms that are switched on (environment,
negative and positive density dependence), $w_{ij} \in [0, 1]$ is the fitness
term of mechanism $j$ (see Environmental filtering and Density
dependence) and $m$ = `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio`. Through
each mechanism, an individual with $w_{ij} = 0$ thus dies $m$ times as often
as one with $w_{ij} = 1$, and the rates of several mechanisms multiply
(proportional hazards). As the number of deaths per generation is fixed, only
relative rates matter: a term that is equal for all individuals has no effect,
and with $m = 1$ the model is neutral if fitness acts only on mortality. With a
single mechanism (or only the Red Queen), the model uses a different rule:
every $m$-th draw kills, all other draws kill with probability $1 - w_i$;
without the Red Queen, this gives the same ratios of death rates.

Fitness can also act on the replacement:

- **Reproduction** (`"reproduction"`): the dispersal weights of the potential
  parents are multiplied by their fitness in their own cells. With global
  dispersal, this is possible only without environment, density dependence
  and Red Queen.
- **Recruitment** (`"recruitment"`): the offspring of a drawn parent is
  established only with a probability given by its fitness in the free cell,
  evaluated with the traits of the parent and the neighbors of that cell;
  otherwise another parent is drawn. After as many rejections as there are
  possible parents (at most 1000), the parent is drawn directly with
  probabilities proportional to dispersal weight times fitness. The parents
  within dispersal range thus compete in a weighted lottery for the cell, so
  recruitment has no effect if they all have the same fitness there.

The stages can be combined, e.g. `fitnessActsOn = c("mortality",
"recruitment")`; `"both"` is short for mortality and reproduction. The fitness
terms then act at each of these stages.

On reproduction and recruitment, the terms of several mechanisms multiply. The
Red Queen bonus (see Speciation) multiplies fitness.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fitnessActsOn` | stages on which fitness acts | `"mortality"` | `"mortality"`, `"reproduction"`, `"recruitment"`, a combination of them, or `"both"` (restrictions: see Reproduction below and Red Queen in Speciation) |
| `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio` | ratio $m$ of the death rates at fitness terms 0 and 1, for each mechanism acting on mortality | 10 | integer $\ge 1$; 1: no selection through mortality |

Table: Arguments of `createCompletePar()` for selection.

### Strength of selection

`fitnessBaseMortalityRatio` sets how strongly fitness acts on mortality: the
ratio of the death rates of individuals with fitness terms 0 and 1. The
simulations vary it from 1 to 50, with full environmental filtering
(`environment = 1`) or full density dependence (`negativeDD = 1`).

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 1`, the model is neutral
here (fitness acts only on mortality). We therefore expect the effects of environmental filtering
and density dependence to increase with `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio`, starting
from the neutral values.
:::

```{r selection, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against fitnessBaseMortalityRatio (logarithmic axis), with full environmental filtering (environment = 1) or full negative density dependence (negativeDD = 1), fitness acting on mortality, dispersal 1, 50 × 50 cells.", capRuns("selection", ref = FALSE))}
sel <- main
sel$settings$scenario <- ifelse(sel$settings$environment > 0, "environment", "negativeDD")
response(sel, "selection", "fitnessBaseMortalityRatio", group = "scenario", log = "x")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** With `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 1`, both scenarios give the values
of the neutral model with local dispersal, as expected. With environmental
filtering, the correlation between trait and environment is almost perfect
already at 2
(`r val("selection", "corTraitEnv", environment = 1, fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 2)`),
and richness keeps increasing up to the largest value
(`r val("selection", "richness", environment = 1, fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 50, digits = 3)`
species at 50). At 50, the gamma statistic drops and the Colless index becomes
positive; the reason is unknown. With density dependence, richness increases
only slowly (to
`r val("selection", "richness", density = 1, fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 50, digits = 3)`
species at 50), whereas the share of conspecific neighbors keeps decreasing, and
the competition trait splits into two groups already at 2 (see Negative density
dependence).
:::

### Life stage of selection

`fitnessActsOn` sets the life stages on which fitness acts: mortality,
reproduction, recruitment or a combination (`"both"` is mortality and
reproduction). The simulations compare mortality, reproduction, both and
recruitment with full environmental filtering or full density dependence.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** On mortality, unfit individuals
die more often, with a ratio set by `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio`; on
reproduction and recruitment, fitness enters directly as a weight, so the
strength of selection differs between the stages. Selection on recruitment
evaluates the offspring in its new cell, so environmental filtering should act
there like a habitat filter; density dependence on recruitment compares the
offspring with the neighbors of that cell. We therefore expect effects in the
same direction at all stages, but of different strength; we found no
prediction in the literature for this.
:::

```{r fitnessactson, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the life stage on which fitness acts (mortality, reproduction, both: mortality and reproduction, recruitment), with environmental filtering (environment = 1) or density dependence (negativeDD = 1); dispersal 1, 50 × 50 cells.", capRuns("fitnessActsOn", ref = FALSE))}
fa <- main
fa$settings$scenario <- ifelse(fa$settings$environment > 0, "environment", "negativeDD")
response(fa, "fitnessActsOn", "fitnessActsOn", group = "scenario", xlab = "",
         xnames = c(mortality = "mort.", reproduction = "repr.", both = "both", recruitment = "recr."))
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** With environmental filtering, traits match the environment at all
stages, but richness increases much more when fitness acts on mortality
(`r val("fitnessActsOn", "richness", environment = 1, fitnessActsOn = "mortality", digits = 3)`
species) than on reproduction
(`r val("fitnessActsOn", "richness", environment = 1, fitnessActsOn = "reproduction", digits = 3)`)
or recruitment
(`r val("fitnessActsOn", "richness", environment = 1, fitnessActsOn = "recruitment", digits = 3)`).
Contrary to the expectation, the stages do not all act in the same direction:
on mortality, filtering slightly lowers the share of conspecific neighbors
compared with the neutral model, on reproduction and recruitment it raises it.
With density dependence, richness hardly differs between the stages, but on
recruitment, density dependence almost removes conspecific neighbors (share
`r val("fitnessActsOn", "conspecificNeighbors", density = 1, fitnessActsOn = "recruitment")`,
on mortality
`r val("fitnessActsOn", "conspecificNeighbors", density = 1, fitnessActsOn = "mortality")`),
probably because each offspring is compared directly with the neighbors of the
cell it would settle in.
:::

## Speciation

The default speciation mechanism is point speciation: in each generation, the
number of new species is drawn from a Poisson distribution with mean
`specRate`, and for each of them an individual is chosen at random. `specRate`
is thus the expected number of new species per generation in the whole grid,
not a rate per individual. The founding individual keeps its traits, which
become the initial trait means of the new species (see Known limitations).

All speciation mechanisms implemented in the model are summarized below:

- **Point speciation:** the default, see above.
- **Fission type 1:** an individual is drawn at random, so that species are
  chosen in proportion to their abundance; every second individual of its
  species becomes part of a new species.
- **Fission type 2:** as type 1, but the species is split geographically at the
  mean x-coordinate of its individuals. One part becomes a new species, the
  other part is not affected.
- **Protracted speciation:** based on @rosindell2010, a species undergoes an
  incipient stage before becoming a new species. In the implementation, the
  chosen individual becomes a new species only if it survives `protracted`
  generations; its offspring do not inherit the incipient state (see Known
  limitations). `specRate` is
  then the expected number of incipient individuals per generation.
- **Red Queen:** based on @odwyer2014, new species have advantages over old
  species due to their novelty alone, and the effect vanishes over time. The
  fitness is multiplied by $1 + s \exp(-q\,a)$, where $s$ = `redQueenStrength`,
  $q$ = `redQueen` and $a$ is the number of generations since the species arose,
  minus one; without environment and density dependence, the base fitness is
  set to 0.01. With several mechanisms on mortality, the death rate is divided
  by this factor instead. The bonus does not act on recruitment (so `fitnessActsOn = "recruitment"`
  alone gives an error with the Red Queen), and on reproduction only together
  with environment or density dependence.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `specRate` | expected number of new species per generation in the whole grid | 1 | $\ge 0$, $\le x \cdot y$ |
| `fission` | speciation by fission: 0 (none), 1 or 2 | 0 | 0, 1, 2 |
| `protracted` | generations an incipient species must survive | 0 | integer $\ge 0$ |
| `redQueenStrength`, `redQueen` | strength $s$ and decay $q$ of the novelty advantage | 0, 0 | $\ge 0$ |

Table: Arguments of `createCompletePar()` for speciation.

### Neutral model and speciation rate

The neutral model, without fitness differences and with point speciation, is
the reference for all other processes. The simulations vary
`specRate` from 0.5 to 8 on grids of 20, 50 and 100 cells per side with global
dispersal.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With global dispersal and no fitness differences, the model
is a zero-sum Moran model: in each generation, $J = x \cdot y$ individuals die
and are replaced by offspring of random individuals, and on average `specRate`
of the replacements found a new species, so the speciation probability per
replacement is $\nu = \texttt{specRate}/J$. (In `runSimulation()`, the new
species arise at the end of each generation rather than at single
replacements, so the model is close to, but not exactly, a Moran model.) The
equilibrium of the Moran model is known exactly [@vallade2003]. The number of
species follows the Ewens sampling formula [@ewens1972],
$$E(S) = \sum_{i=0}^{J-1} \frac{\theta}{\theta + i}, \qquad
\theta = \frac{(J-1)\,\nu}{1-\nu} \approx \texttt{specRate}.$$
For large $J$ and small $\nu$, this $\theta$ is about half of the fundamental
biodiversity number $2J\nu$ used in other formulations of neutral theory
[@hubbell2001; @vallade2003]; `es()` uses $2J\nu$ (see Known limitations). The
same theory predicts that two random individuals belong to the same species
with probability $1/(1+\theta)$. With global dispersal, space plays no role, so
this is also the expected share of conspecific neighbors. The theory also gives
the expected abundance distribution [@vallade2003], which we compare with the
rank–abundance curve of the model.

For the tree of the extant species, neutral theory predicts more imbalance
than a Yule tree, because the speciation probability of a species is
proportional to its abundance [@davies2011; @manceau2015]. The
Yule-normalized Colless index is close to 0 for Yule trees [@blum2006], so we
expect positive values. Neutral models in equilibrium are not expected to show
the slowdown of branching towards the present (negative gamma statistic) that
is typical of empirical trees [@davies2011; @manceau2015; @phillimore2008].
:::

```{r neutral, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = paste0("Neutral model with global dispersal against the speciation rate, for three grid sizes, at the end of runs of ", fmt(gens[["neutral"]]), " generations (mean and 95% confidence interval of ", reps, " replicate runs). Left: species richness; dashed: Ewens sampling formula, dotted: es(). Right: share of conspecific neighbors; dashed: 1/(1 + θ).")}
op <- style(mfrow = c(1, 2))
f <- final(main, "neutral", "richness")
g <- final(main, "neutral", "conspecificNeighbors")
sizes <- sort(unique(f$x))
sr <- exp(seq(log(min(f$specRate)), log(max(f$specRate)), length.out = 30))
sc <- groupCols(sizes)
plot(f$specRate, f$mean, type = "n", log = "xy", xlab = "specRate", xaxt = "n",
     ylab = "Species richness", ylim = range(c(pmax(f$mean - f$ci, 1), 2 * f$mean), na.rm = TRUE))
axis(1, at = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), labels = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8))
for (k in seq_along(sizes)) {
  s <- f[f$x == sizes[k], ]
  points(s$specRate, s$mean, col = sc[k], pch = 16)
  ciBars(s$specRate, s$mean, s$ci, sc[k])
  lines(sr, sapply(sr, function(r) ewens(theta(r, sizes[k]^2), sizes[k]^2)), col = sc[k], lty = 2)
  lines(sr, sapply(sr, es, dimensions = sizes[k]), col = sc[k], lty = 3)
}
legend("topleft", legend = paste(sizes, "x", sizes), col = sc,
       pch = 16, bty = "n")
plot(g$specRate, g$mean, type = "n", log = "x", xlab = "specRate", xaxt = "n",
     ylab = "Conspecific neighbors", ylim = c(0, 1))
axis(1, at = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), labels = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8))
for (k in seq_along(sizes)) {
  s <- g[g$x == sizes[k], ]
  points(s$specRate, s$mean, col = sc[k], pch = 16)
  ciBars(s$specRate, s$mean, s$ci, sc[k])
  lines(sr, 1 / (1 + theta(sr, sizes[k]^2)), col = sc[k], lty = 2)
}
par(op)
```

```{r neutral-rac, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = paste0("Rank–abundance curve of the neutral model with global dispersal (50 × 50 cells, specRate = 2; replicate mean at generation ", fmt(gens[["neutral"]]), ") and the expectation from the Ewens sampling formula (dashed).")}
s <- settingId(main, "neutral", specRate = 2, x = 50)
r <- main$rac[main$rac$block == "neutral" & main$rac$setting == s, ]
r <- r[order(r$rank), ]
set.seed(1)
e <- ewensRac(theta(2, 2500), 2500)
style(mar = c(3.4, 4.4, 1.6, 0.6))
plot(r$rank, r$mean, log = "y", pch = 16, col = "grey50", xlab = "Rank", yaxt = "n",
     ylab = "", xlim = range(c(r$rank, seq_along(e))), ylim = c(0.5, max(r$mean, e)))
title(ylab = "Abundance", line = 3.2)
logAxis(2)
lines(seq_along(e)[e >= 0.5], e[e >= 0.5], lty = 2)
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** The share of conspecific neighbors and the rank–abundance curve
agree with the Ewens sampling formula. Species richness is higher than expected
in most settings, by up to about 15%, but within the 95% confidence interval in
more than half of them (e.g.
`r val("neutral", "richness", x = 50, specRate = 8, digits = 3)` instead of
`r round(ewens(theta(8, 2500), 2500), 1)` for 50 × 50 cells and `specRate = 8`),
possibly because of the batch speciation described above
([#124](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/124)). `es()`
gives 40–80% more species than the simulations, as expected from its definition
of $\theta$. As predicted, the Colless index is
positive in all settings. The gamma statistic is positive and increases with the
speciation rate, i.e. the trees show more recent than early branching.
:::

### Protracted speciation and Red Queen

Two mechanisms change whether new species persist: protracted speciation
completes a speciation only if the founding individual survives `protracted`
generations (see Known limitations), and the Red Queen gives young species a
fitness advantage (`redQueenStrength`, decaying with `redQueen`). The
simulations vary `protracted` from 0 to 5, and use `redQueen = 0.01` and `0.1`
with `redQueenStrength = 100`.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** An individual survives a generation with probability of about $\exp(-1)$, so in the
neutral model protracted speciation should act like a speciation rate reduced
by a factor of about $\exp(-p)$, with $p$ = `protracted`, and richness should decrease accordingly. In
the original model of protracted speciation, in which the whole incipient
lineage becomes a new species [@rosindell2010], protracted speciation slows down branching towards the present
[@etienne2012]. A Red Queen advantage of young species is expected to make
species younger without changing abundance distributions much
[@odwyer2014]. Without environment and density dependence, the base fitness is
0.01, so `redQueenStrength` must be large (here 100) for young species to
survive the fitness-dependent draws noticeably more often.
:::

```{r protracted, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the number of generations an incipient species must survive (protracted), with specRate = 2, dispersal 1 and 50 × 50 cells.", capRuns("speciation", fewer = TRUE))}
response(main, "speciation", "protracted",
         settings = settingId(main, "speciation", redQueen = 0))
```

```{r protracted-ratio, echo = FALSE}
# richness relative to protracted = 0: simulated and Ewens with specRate * exp(-p)
rich <- function(p) val("speciation", "richness", protracted = p, redQueen = 0, digits = 10)
ewensRatio <- function(p) ewens(theta(2, 2500) * exp(-p), 2500) / ewens(theta(2, 2500), 2500)
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Richness decreases with `protracted` roughly as predicted by a
speciation rate reduced by $\exp(-p)$, slightly more: relative to
`protracted = 0`, it is
`r round(rich(1) / rich(0), 2)` for $p = 1$ (Ewens sampling formula, which assumes global dispersal, with the
reduced rate: `r round(ewensRatio(1), 2)`) and `r round(rich(2) / rich(0), 2)` for
$p = 2$ (`r round(ewensRatio(2), 2)`). With $p = 5$, most runs end with a single
species. The Red Queen advantage more than doubles richness
(`r val("speciation", "richness", redQueen = 0.01, digits = 3)` and
`r val("speciation", "richness", redQueen = 0.1, digits = 3)` species instead of
`r val("speciation", "richness", redQueen = 0, protracted = 0, digits = 3)`) and
strongly increases Shannon diversity, so it changes the abundance distribution
more than expected.
:::

### Fission

With `fission`, a new species arises by splitting an existing species instead
of from a single individual. The simulations compare the two types of fission
with point speciation.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Fission as a mode of speciation in neutral models is
described by @hubbell2001. Unlike point
speciation, a new species starts with many individuals, so it rarely goes
extinct soon after its origin. We therefore expect fewer rare species, more
even abundances and older species than with point speciation at the same
`specRate`. Whether richness is higher or lower is not obvious: new species
survive longer, but each fission also takes individuals from an existing
species (half of them with type 1). With local
dispersal, the two daughter species of type 1 are mixed in space, so the
share of conspecific neighbors should decrease; the daughter species of
type 2 occupy separate parts of their parent's range, so the share of
conspecific neighbors should change little. For tree shape, we found no prediction.
:::

```{r fission, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators for point speciation (none; the reference setting) and the two types of fission (dispersal 1, specRate = 2, 50 × 50 cells).", capRuns("fission"))}
response(withSettings(main, "fission", "dispersal", dispersal = "1"), "fission", "fission", discrete = TRUE, xlab = "",
         xnames = c("0" = "none", "1" = "type 1", "2" = "type 2"),
         indicators = c("richness", "evenness", "dominance", "conspecificNeighbors", "colless", "gamma", "sdCompetitionTrait"))
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Both types of fission give more than four times as many species as
point speciation at the same `specRate`
(`r val("fission", "richness", fission = 1, digits = 3)` and
`r val("fission", "richness", fission = 2, digits = 3)` instead of
`r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "1", digits = 3)`), with much more
even abundances, as expected. Contrary to the expectation, the species are
much younger (mean age, estimated from the species IDs, see Species ages:
`r val("fission", "meanSpeciesAge", fission = 1)` and
`r val("fission", "meanSpeciesAge", fission = 2)` instead of
`r val("speciation", "meanSpeciesAge", protracted = 0, redQueen = 0)` generations).
A likely explanation: nearly every new species survives its origin, so about
2 species are added per generation, and richness divided by 2 (about 45
generations) roughly matches the mean age. With point speciation, most new species go
extinct within a few generations, and the few that persist are old. Both types of fission reduce
the share of conspecific neighbors; for type 2, this is contrary to the
expectation. They also make the trees more balanced and increase the gamma
statistic.
:::

### Comparing speciation mechanisms

The mechanisms differ in how many species they produce at a given `specRate`,
and many patterns change with richness alone. To separate the effect of the
mechanism from that of richness, each mechanism was run over a range of
speciation rates (dispersal 1), and the indicators are compared at the
richness they reach.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** If a mechanism acts only through the number of species, its
indicators lie on the same curve against richness as those of point
speciation. Deviations show effects of the mechanism itself: more even
abundances and older species with fission, whose new species start with many
individuals, and younger species with the Red Queen advantage. Protracted
speciation, which in this implementation only lowers the effective speciation
rate (see Protracted speciation and Red Queen), should lie on the curve of
point speciation.
:::

```{r mechanisms, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste0("Speciation mechanisms at dispersal 1: species richness against specRate (first panel), and other indicators against richness (means of ", reps, " replicate runs at generation ", fmt(gens[["speciationRate"]]), ", fewer for tree statistics in some settings, see Simulation design; specRate from 0.5 to 8, 50 × 50 cells).")}
# final values of an indicator for each speciation mechanism and specRate
mechanisms <- function(indicator) {
  get <- function(block, ...) {
    f <- final(main, block, indicator)
    v <- list(...)
    for (n in names(v)) f <- f[f[[n]] == v[[n]], ]
    f
  }
  point <- rbind(get("specRateLocal"), get("dispersal", dispersal = "1"))
  point$mechanism <- "point"
  other <- rbind(get("speciationRate"), get("fission"), get("speciation", redQueen = 0.01),
                 get("speciation", protracted = 1, redQueen = 0), get("speciation", protracted = 2, redQueen = 0))
  other$mechanism <- ifelse(other$fission > 0, paste("fission", other$fission),
                            ifelse(other$protracted > 0, paste("protracted", other$protracted), "Red Queen"))
  rbind(point, other)[c("block", "setting", "mechanism", "specRate", "mean")]
}
mechs <- c("point", "fission 1", "fission 2", "protracted 1", "protracted 2", "Red Queen")
mr <- mechanisms("richness")
op <- style(mfrow = c(2, 4))
plot(mr$specRate, mr$mean, type = "n", log = "xy", xlab = "specRate", ylab = "", xaxt = "n",
     main = labels[["richness"]])
axis(1, at = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), labels = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8))
for (k in seq_along(mechs)) {
  r <- mr[mr$mechanism == mechs[k], ]
  r <- r[order(r$specRate), ]
  lines(r$specRate, r$mean, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[k])
}
for (ind in c("shannon", "conspecificNeighbors", "sdCompetitionTrait", "colless", "gamma")) {
  m <- merge(mechanisms(ind), mr, by = c("block", "setting", "mechanism", "specRate"),
             suffixes = c("", ".richness"))
  plot(m$mean.richness, m$mean, type = "n", log = "x", xlab = "Species richness", ylab = "",
       main = labels[[ind]])
  for (k in seq_along(mechs)) {
    r <- m[m$mechanism == mechs[k], ]
    r <- r[order(r$mean.richness), ]
    lines(r$mean.richness, r$mean, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[k])
  }
}
legendPanel(legend = mechs, col = cols, lty = 1, pch = 16, title = "speciation")
par(op)
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** As expected, protracted speciation lies on the curves of point
speciation. Fission and the Red Queen do not: at the same richness, both give
higher Shannon diversity, i.e. more even abundances, more balanced trees
(lower Colless index) and a lower gamma statistic than point speciation. They
differ in spatial structure: at the same richness, fission gives fewer
conspecific neighbors than point speciation, and the Red Queen more. (At the
same `specRate`, fission increases the gamma statistic, see Fission, in line with
its much higher richness.) The curves of fission overlap those of point
speciation only at `specRate = 0.5`, so for fission the comparison rests on few
settings.
:::

## Known limitations

::: {.limitation}
Some properties of the current implementation can be unexpected; they are
discussed in the issues of the package repository:

- `dispersal` has an effect only in steps of 0.5
  ([#141](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/141)).
- With protracted speciation, the offspring of an incipient individual do not
  inherit the incipient state
  ([#143](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/143)).
- New species keep the traits of their founding individual; a trait change at
  speciation is not implemented
  ([#114](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/114)).
- With the trait kernels (`negativeDDKernel = "absolute"` or `"gaussian"`),
  density dependence develops only after thousands of generations, so short
  runs show little of its effect; the `"species"` kernel acts from the first
  speciation on
  ([#133](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/133)).
- `es()` calculates the expected number of species of the neutral model with
  $\theta = 2 \cdot$ `specRate`, about twice the value that fits the model
  (see Neutral model and speciation rate;
  [#124](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/124)).
:::

# Community patterns

This chapter compares the patterns across processes. Its sections on
richness, spatial structure, traits and phylogeny follow the plot and summary
functions of the vignette "EcoPhyloSim user guide".

## Overview of effects

The figure summarizes the effects of single changes of the parameters,
starting from the reference setting (for density dependence, from the same
setting run for 100,000 generations) or, for parameters that act only together
with another process, from a setting with that process. Significance is
tested with Welch's t-test (false discovery rate of 5% over all cells). The
sections of the chapter Processes and below show the full responses.

```{r effects, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.8, fig.cap = "Standardized effects of single parameter changes (rows) on the indicators (columns) at the end of the runs: difference of the replicate means divided by the pooled standard deviation between replicates (▲ increase, ▼ decrease, number: size; light blue: decrease, light orange: increase, saturating at ±3); empty: not significant (false discovery rate 5%); –: not defined."}
ref <- list("dispersal", dispersal = "1")
contrasts <- list(
  "dispersal 1 to 3" = list(ref, list("dispersal", dispersal = "3")),
  "dispersal 1 to global" = list(ref, list("dispersal", dispersal = "global")),
  "environment 0 to 1" = list(ref, list("environment", environment = 1, dispersal = "1")),
  "nicheWidth 0.037 to 0.3 (env. 1)" = list(list("nicheWidth", nicheWidth = 0.03659906, dispersal = "1"),
                                            list("nicheWidth", nicheWidth = 0.3, dispersal = "1")),
