  "negativeDD 0 to 1 (radius 1)" = list(list("density", density = 0, densityCut = 1),
                                     list("density", density = 1, densityCut = 1)),
  "negativeDD 0 to 1 (radius 2)" = list(list("density", density = 0, densityCut = 2),
                                     list("density", density = 1, densityCut = 2)),
  "kernel absolute to species (negativeDD 1)" = list(list("density", density = 1, densityCut = 1),
                                                  list("densityKernel", density = 1, negativeDDKernel = "species")),
  "positiveDD 0 to 0.05 (radius 2)" = list(list("density", density = 0, densityCut = 1),
                                           list("positiveDD", positiveDD = 0.05, density = 0)),
  "fitnessBaseMort. 10 to 50 (env. 1)" = list(list("selection", environment = 1, fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 10),
                                              list("selection", environment = 1, fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 50)),
  "specRate 2 to 8" = list(ref, list("specRateLocal", specRate = 8)),
  "protracted 0 to 5" = list(ref, list("speciation", protracted = 5)),
  "redQueen 0 to 0.1 (strength 100)" = list(ref, list("speciation", redQueen = 0.1)),
  "fission: none to type 1" = list(ref, list("fission", fission = 1)),
  "grid 50 × 50 to 100 × 100" = list(ref, list("gridSize", x = 100)))
# final values of an indicator in a setting given by block and parameter values
pick <- function(x, ind) {
  f <- final(main, x[[1]], ind)
  f[f$setting == do.call(settingId, c(list(main), x)), ]
}
eff <- lapply(contrasts, function(k) sapply(core, function(ind) {
  a <- pick(k[[1]], ind)
  b <- pick(k[[2]], ind)
  if (nrow(a) != 1 || nrow(b) != 1) return(c(NA, NA))
  va <- a$sd^2 / a$n
  vb <- b$sd^2 / b$n
  c((b$mean - a$mean) / sqrt((a$sd^2 + b$sd^2) / 2),     # standardized effect
    2 * pt(-abs(b$mean - a$mean) / sqrt(va + vb),        # Welch test
           (va + vb)^2 / (va^2 / (a$n - 1) + vb^2 / (b$n - 1))))
}))
efs <- t(sapply(eff, `[`, 1, ))
efs[!is.finite(efs)] <- NA
# p-values adjusted for the false discovery rate over all cells
padj <- matrix(p.adjust(t(sapply(eff, `[`, 2, )), "BH"), nrow(efs))
op <- par(mar = c(0.5, 16, 6, 5), cex = 0.75)
cap <- 3
# light tints of the figure colors (blue: decrease, orange: increase), at most 55% at |effect| >= cap
tint <- function(hex, a) rgb(t(1 - a * (1 - col2rgb(hex) / 255)))
z <- pmax(pmin(efs, cap), -cap)
sig <- !is.na(efs) & !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05
cl <- matrix("white", nrow(efs), ncol(efs))
cl[sig] <- vapply(z[sig], function(v) tint(if (v < 0) "#0072B2" else "#D55E00", 0.55 * abs(v) / cap), "")
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, ncol(efs) + 0.5), ylim = c(nrow(efs) + 0.5, 0.5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
rect(col(efs) - 0.5, row(efs) - 0.5, col(efs) + 0.5, row(efs) + 0.5, col = cl, border = "grey85")
if (any(sig)) {
  points(col(efs)[sig] - 0.25, row(efs)[sig], pch = ifelse(efs[sig] > 0, 24, 25), bg = "grey20", col = "grey20", cex = 0.9)
  text(col(efs)[sig] + 0.1, row(efs)[sig], sprintf("%.1f", abs(efs[sig])), cex = 0.85, col = "grey10")
}
if (anyNA(efs)) text(col(efs)[is.na(efs)], row(efs)[is.na(efs)], "–", col = "grey50")
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(efs)), labels = rownames(efs), las = 1, tick = FALSE, line = -0.8)
text(seq_len(ncol(efs)), 0.3, labels[core], srt = 45, adj = 0, xpd = TRUE)
par(op)
```

## Grid size and shape

The number of cells sets the number of individuals in the community. The
simulations use square grids of 20, 50 and 100 cells per side and, for the
shape, grids of 49 × 49 and 50 × 40 cells with environmental filtering
(`environment = 1`), compared with 50 × 50 cells.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the neutral model, richness increases roughly with the
logarithm of the number of individuals (Ewens sampling formula). With local
dispersal, larger grids also contain more spatially separated clusters
[@durrett1996], so richness should increase faster. The shape of the grid
should matter only through its number of cells and, with environmental
filtering, through the environmental gradient along the x-axis (which differs
for an odd number of columns, see Environmental filtering). A
grid of 50 × 40 cells should thus differ from 50 × 50 cells only as expected
from 20% fewer cells.
:::

```{r gridsize, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the number of cells per side of square grids, with dispersal 1 and specRate = 2.", capRuns("gridSize"))}
response(main, "gridSize", "x", xlab = "Grid size (cells per side)")
```

```{r gridshape, echo = FALSE}
shape <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("richness", "corTraitEnv", "conspecificNeighbors"), function(ind) {
  f <- rbind(final(main, "gridShape", ind), final(main, "environment", ind))
  f <- f[f$environment == 1 & f$dispersal == "1", ]
  data.frame(grid = paste(f$x, "×", f$y), indicator = labels[[ind]],
             value = sprintf("%.3g ± %.2g", f$mean, f$ci))
}))
knitr::kable(reshape(shape, idvar = "grid", timevar = "indicator", direction = "wide"),
             col.names = c("Grid", unique(shape$indicator)), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Indicators for grids of different shape with environmental filtering (environment = 1, dispersal 1; replicate mean ± 95% confidence interval).")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** With local dispersal, richness increases from
`r val("gridSize", "richness", x = 20, digits = 3)` to
`r val("gridSize", "richness", x = 100, digits = 3)` species between 20 × 20 and
100 × 100 cells, faster than in the neutral model with global dispersal (from
`r val("neutral", "richness", x = 20, specRate = 2, digits = 3)` to
`r val("neutral", "richness", x = 100, specRate = 2, digits = 3)`), as expected.
With environmental filtering, the grid of 49 × 49 cells gives the same values as
50 × 50 cells, so the slightly different gradient of an odd number of columns
does not matter here. The grid of 50 × 40 cells has about 10% fewer species,
with the same correlation between trait and environment and the same share of
conspecific neighbors; whether this is what 20% fewer cells imply cannot be
judged here, as the runs on grids of different size have no environmental
filtering.
:::

## Species richness and abundances

Species richness (`specRich()`) and the rank–abundance curve (`rac()`) of the
neutral model are compared with the Ewens sampling formula in the section
Neutral model and speciation rate; the overview figure shows which processes
change them.

Richness increases with local dispersal, environmental filtering (most with
local dispersal and strong selection on mortality), density dependence by
species identity, the Red Queen advantage and fission. It decreases with
protracted speciation and with positive density dependence. Density dependence
on the competition trait increases it only slightly at dispersal 1 and above,
but more with shorter dispersal. Shannon diversity mostly follows richness, but
environmental filtering, density dependence by species identity, fission and
the Red Queen make abundances more even than point speciation does at the same
richness (see Comparing speciation mechanisms).

## Spatial structure

The share of conspecific neighbors and the species–area curve (`sac()`)
describe how the species are distributed in space. Dispersal limitation creates
clusters of conspecifics (see Dispersal), and density dependence changes their
size (see Density dependence).

Without positive density dependence, local dispersal is the main source of
aggregation: with dispersal 1, about
`r round(100 * val("dispersal", "conspecificNeighbors", dispersal = "1"))`% of
the neighbors are conspecific, with global dispersal
`r round(100 * val("dispersal", "conspecificNeighbors", dispersal = "global"))`%.
Negative density dependence reduces aggregation, most when it acts on
recruitment or uses the `"species"` kernel; positive density dependence alone
makes almost all neighbors conspecific. Environmental filtering with the default
niche width, acting on mortality, reduces aggregation strongly with global
dispersal and slightly with local dispersal; with wider niches or acting on
reproduction or recruitment, it increases it with local dispersal.
With local dispersal, the species–area curve is flatter at small areas and
steeper at large areas than with global dispersal.

## Traits and environment

`plotTraitDistribution()` shows the traits against the environment. The
correlation between the environmental trait and the environment measures how
well species are sorted along the gradient (see Environmental filtering), the
spread of the competition trait how far competition drives traits apart (see
Density dependence).

Whenever environmental filtering acts with local dispersal, traits match the
environment almost perfectly, at all niche widths, life stages and strengths of
selection from 2 on; with global dispersal, the correlation stays below 0.6
(mass effects). The spread of the competition trait shows whether density
dependence acts on it (see Similarity measure of density dependence).
Environmental filtering also
increases the spread of the competition and neutral traits, which are not under
selection, possibly because there are more and older species whose traits have
drifted apart.

## Phylogeny

The tree of the extant species is summarized by the Colless index
(`collessImbalance()`) and the gamma statistic, and the age of its species by
their mean age and its correlation with abundance. The sections of the chapter
Processes show the effects on the tree.

The trees of the neutral model are less balanced than Yule trees (positive
Colless index). In most settings, environmental filtering, density dependence,
fission and the Red Queen advantage make them more balanced (Colless index
around or below 0). The gamma statistic is not clearly negative in any setting,
i.e. none of the processes produces the slowdown of branching towards the
present that is typical of empirical trees. It tends to increase with richness,
but fission, the Red Queen advantage, environmental filtering combined with
density dependence or acting on reproduction, and very strong selection
(`fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 50`) give lower values than point speciation at
the same richness, and it is low wherever there are few species (low speciation rates,
protracted speciation, positive density dependence).

### Species ages

The age of a species is estimated from its ID: species are numbered in the
order of their origin, and new species arise at a roughly constant rate, so the
age of species $i$ at generation $G$ is about $G(1 - i/i_{max})$, where
$i_{max}$ is the largest ID in the phylogeny. The figure uses the neutral model
with global dispersal (50 × 50 cells) and the runs of Protracted speciation and
Red Queen.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In neutral models, species persist for a long time, longer
than observed in nature [@chisholm2014], and since species start with one
individual and grow by drift, abundant species are on average older.
:::

```{r ages, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = paste0("Mean species age (left) and rank correlation between age and abundance (right) at the end of the runs (mean and 95% confidence interval of ", reps, " replicate runs, fewer for the rank correlation in some settings; see Simulation design). Circles: neutral model with global dispersal against the speciation rate (50 × 50 cells). At specRate = 2, for dispersal = 1: without (square) and with a Red Queen advantage (triangles).")}
op <- style(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 4.4, 1.6, 0.6))
for (ind in c("meanSpeciesAge", "corAgeAbundance")) {
  f <- final(main, "neutral", ind)
  f <- f[f$x == 50, ]
  sp <- final(main, "speciation", ind)
  sp <- sp[sp$protracted == 0, ]
  sp <- sp[order(sp$redQueen), ]
  xs <- 2 * 1.12^seq_len(nrow(sp)) # next to the neutral point at specRate = 2
  cs <- cols[1 + seq_len(nrow(sp))]
  yr <- range(c(f$mean - f$ci, f$mean + f$ci, sp$mean - sp$ci, sp$mean + sp$ci), na.rm = TRUE)
  if (ind == "meanSpeciesAge") yr[2] <- yr[2] + 0.5 * diff(yr) # room for the legend
  plot(f$specRate, f$mean, log = "x", pch = 16, col = "grey50", ylim = yr, xlab = "specRate", xaxt = "n",
       xlim = range(c(f$specRate, xs)),
       ylab = "")
  title(ylab = if (ind == "meanSpeciesAge") "Mean species age (generations)" else "Cor(age, abundance)", line = 3.2)
  axis(1, at = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), labels = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8))
  ciBars(f$specRate, f$mean, f$ci, "grey50")
  points(xs, sp$mean, pch = ifelse(sp$redQueen > 0, 17, 15), col = cs)
  ciBars(xs, sp$mean, sp$ci, cs)
  if (ind == "meanSpeciesAge")
    legend("topright", legend = c("neutral, global", paste("dispersal 1, redQueen =", sp$redQueen)),
           pch = c(16, ifelse(sp$redQueen > 0, 17, 15)), col = c("grey50", cs), bty = "n")
}
par(op)
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** In the neutral model, mean species age decreases with the speciation
rate, and abundant species are older (rank correlation about
`r val("neutral", "corAgeAbundance", x = 50, specRate = 2, digits = 1)`), as
expected. The Red Queen advantage reduces the mean species age from
`r val("speciation", "meanSpeciesAge", redQueen = 0, protracted = 0, digits = 3)` to
about `r val("speciation", "meanSpeciesAge", redQueen = 0.01)` generations and
removes most of the correlation between age and abundance.
:::

## Interactions of processes

### Environment and density dependence combined

The simulations combine `environment` and `negativeDD` at 0, 0.5 and 1 each.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Environmental filtering favors similar species in the same
place, and density dependence favors dissimilar neighbors, so the two
processes can mask each other in the patterns [@kraft2015]. Their effects on
the death rate multiply (see Selection), so each acts whatever the
strength of the other.
:::

```{r envdensity, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators against the strength of environmental filtering (environment) for three strengths of negative density dependence (negativeDD; radius 1, kernel \"absolute\"), with dispersal 1 on 50 × 50 cells.", capRuns("envDensity"))}
response(main, "envDensity", "environment", group = "density")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** The two processes do not mask each other in richness, trait sorting
or aggregation: with environmental filtering, density dependence still
increases richness (at `environment = 1` from
`r val("envDensity", "richness", environment = 1, density = 0, digits = 3)` to
`r val("envDensity", "richness", environment = 1, density = 1, digits = 3)`
species), reduces the share of conspecific neighbors and splits the competition
trait as without filtering, and filtering sorts the traits along the gradient at
all strengths of density dependence. They interact in the shape of the tree:
with both processes, the gamma statistic is much lower
(`r val("envDensity", "gamma", environment = 1, density = 1)`) than with
filtering alone (`r val("envDensity", "gamma", environment = 1, density = 0)`) or
density dependence alone (`r val("envDensity", "gamma", environment = 0, density = 1)`),
and the Colless index is close to 0.
:::

### Assembly processes and dispersal

The simulations combine environmental filtering (`environment` = 0 or 1) and
density dependence (`negativeDD` = 0 or 1), each with global dispersal and
dispersal 1.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Environmental filtering should increase richness and the
match between traits and environment, and density dependence should reduce
aggregation and increase richness (see the results of Environmental filtering
and Density dependence). Dispersal can change how strongly each process shows
[@mouquet2003; @adler2005].
:::

```{r assembly, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = paste("Indicators for the four combinations of environmental filtering (environment 0 or 1) and negative density dependence (negativeDD 0 or 1): neutral, env. (filtering only), dens. (density dependence only) and both, with global dispersal and dispersal 1 (50 × 50 cells, specRate = 2).", capRuns("assembly"))}
a <- main$settings$block == "assembly"
main$settings$scenario[a] <- c("neutral", "env.", "dens.", "both")[
  1 + main$settings$environment[a] + 2 * main$settings$density[a]]
response(main, "assembly", "scenario", group = "dispersal", xlab = "")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** Environmental filtering increases richness and the match between
traits and environment, much more with local than with global dispersal.
As in the section Environmental filtering, it does not increase spatial
aggregation (see Spatial structure). Density dependence reduces aggregation with both
types of dispersal, but increases richness only with local dispersal (see
Density dependence and dispersal). With local dispersal, both processes
together give the highest richness (see Environment and density dependence
combined).
:::

## Density dependence measured from mortality

Field studies estimate conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD) from
the mortality of individuals in relation to the number of conspecific
neighbors [@comita2010; @hulsmann2024]. The same can be done with the model
output (`getMortalityData()`): for the last five generations of each run, a
logistic regression of death on the number of conspecifics within a radius of
2 cells, with a separate intercept per species, gives one CNDD coefficient per
run; positive values mean that mortality increases with the number of
conspecific neighbors. It is computed for the runs of Assembly processes and
dispersal.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the neutral model, mortality does not depend on
neighbors, so the coefficient should be close to 0; this is a check of the analysis.
With density dependence, it should be positive. With environmental filtering
and local dispersal, conspecific neighbors indicate suitable habitat, so
mortality may decrease with their number, which would hide density dependence
in such an analysis.
:::

```{r cndd, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = paste0("CNDD coefficient estimated from the last five generations of the runs of the previous figure, per scenario and dispersal (mean and 95% confidence interval of ", reps, " replicate runs; dashed: no effect).")}
f <- merge(main$settings[a, ], main$cndd[main$cndd$block == "assembly", ])
f$ci <- qt(0.975, pmax(f$n - 1, 1)) * f$sd / sqrt(f$n)
f <- f[order(f$density, f$environment, f$dispersal), ]
sc <- unique(f$scenario)
xpos <- match(f$scenario, sc) + ifelse(f$dispersal == "global", -0.1, 0.1)
dc <- groupCols(c("global", "1"), dispersalLevels)
plot(xpos, f$mean, pch = 16, col = dc[f$dispersal], xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "CNDD coefficient", ylim = range(c(0, f$mean - f$ci, f$mean + f$ci)))
axis(1, at = seq_along(sc), labels = sc)
ciBars(xpos, f$mean, f$ci, dc[f$dispersal])
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = names(dc), pch = 16, col = dc, title = "dispersal", bty = "n")
```

::: {.result}
**Result.** As expected, the CNDD coefficient is close to 0 in the neutral model.
With density dependence, it is positive with dispersal 1, but close to 0 with
global dispersal, where density dependence also has little effect on richness
(see Density dependence and dispersal). Environmental filtering makes it
negative, and with both processes it is negative as well, so filtering hides
the density dependence in this analysis. Contrary to the expectation, the
negative effect of filtering is stronger with global than with local dispersal.
:::
